title: Randomness cannot usefully be defined only by the existence of short descriptions

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Randomness cannot usefully be defined only by the existence of short descriptions

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Defining something as random only when no short description of it exists at all is too restrictive and uncomputable (it would mean deterministic rules can never generate randomness), so any useful definition of randomness must refer to how short descriptions are to be found.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Indeed, what I suspect is that ultimately no useful definition of randomness can be based solely on the issue of what short descriptions of something may in principle exist.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Defining the Notion of Randomness” (from p. 552), p. 555. Scope: definitions of randomness, including description-length (algorithmic) definitions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.79

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The formal claims about uncomputability and deterministic generation are accessible to established proof. The recommendation that every useful definition must concern discovery procedures is conceptual and not fully resolved by mathematical results.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Formalize shortest-description randomness as Kolmogorov complexity and prove its uncomputability and the existence of deterministic generators for high-complexity finite outputs. The additional assertion about usefulness would require an explicit practical criterion and cannot be decided by the theorem alone.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Useful' is normative.

Kolmogorov complexity depends on a universal machine up to an additive constant.

Finite deterministic outputs can have different notions of randomness.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The premises are theorems: description-length randomness is uncomputable, and every sequence from a deterministic rule has a short description, so that definition never counts those sequences as random. Those premises can be checked from the published theory now. The further claim that any useful definition must refer to the method of finding descriptions is not a mathematical or empirical proposition.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Treat Kolmogorov complexity as the definition that calls a string random only when it has no short description, and use the known proof that this complexity is uncomputable and infinite for no computable sequence. That confirms the restrictiveness and uncomputability clauses; it does not decide whether every useful definition must mention the search for descriptions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Uncomputability of complexity is compatible with pragmatic randomness tests that never claim to find every short description.

The conclusion about what is useful is a normative judgment about definitions.
